title: Faraday's Notebook
text:
Michael Faraday was born in London in 1791 to a poor family and left school at about thirteen. He became an apprentice to a bookbinder, a job that turned out to be a gift: he spent his spare time reading the books he was supposed to be binding.

When a customer gave him tickets to lectures by the famous chemist Humphry Davy, Faraday took detailed notes, rewrote them neatly and bound them into a book. He then sent this book to Davy, asking for any job in his laboratory. Impressed by the young man's effort, Davy eventually hired him as an assistant.

Faraday went on to make some of the most important discoveries about electricity and magnetism in history, despite having almost no formal education.

Lack of opportunity can hold us back, but showing genuine effort and initiative can open doors that seem firmly closed.

title: The Crow and the Pitcher
text:
During a long, dry summer, a crow was dying of thirst. At last she spotted a tall pitcher standing in a garden. She flew down eagerly, but the water inside was so low that her beak could not reach it.

She tried to tip the pitcher over, but it was far too heavy. She tried to break it, but it was too strong. Many birds would have given up at that point and flown away.

The crow, however, stopped and thought. Then she picked up a small pebble and dropped it into the pitcher. She fetched another, and another. With each stone, the water rose a tiny bit. It was slow, tiring work, but she kept at it. Eventually the water came up high enough for her to drink her fill.

When strength fails, a little creativity and a lot of patience can solve the problem.
source: Kể lại từ ngụ ngôn Aesop

title: Carving a Plough by the Roadside
text:
A young man spent all his savings on a fine piece of wood, planning to carve a plough and sell it. He set up his workshop by the side of a busy road.

An old farmer passed and said, "Make it taller, lad. It will be easier to use." The young man thanked him and carved it taller. Another passer-by said, "Too tall! Make it shorter and smaller." So he shortened it.

Next came a man who claimed that in the mountains people ploughed with elephants. "Make it huge," he advised, "and you will be rich." Excited, the young man reshaped it once more.

By the end of the day, his precious wood had been cut, shaved and recut so many times that it was useless. Nobody could plough with it, and nobody wanted to buy it.

Listening to advice is wise, but we must think for ourselves and stick to a clear purpose, or we will end up pleasing no one.

title: The Doctor Who Asked for Clean Hands
text:
In the 1840s, Ignaz Semmelweis worked in a hospital in Vienna that had two maternity wards. In one, run by doctors, a frighteningly high number of mothers died of fever after giving birth. In the other, run by midwives, far fewer died.

Semmelweis noticed that the doctors often came straight from examining dead bodies to deliver babies. He suspected they were carrying something deadly on their hands. When he insisted that staff wash their hands in a chlorine solution, the death rate fell dramatically.

Surprisingly, many senior doctors rejected his idea. They were offended at the suggestion that they themselves were spreading disease. Semmelweis was largely ignored during his lifetime, and his ideas were only widely accepted years after his death.

Evidence does not always win immediately. Pride and habit can make people resist the truth, even when lives are at stake.

title: Marie Curie's Shed
text:
In the late 1890s, Marie and Pierre Curie suspected that a mineral called pitchblende contained an unknown radioactive element. Proving it, however, meant extracting a tiny amount of the substance from tonnes of raw material.

They had no proper laboratory. Instead they worked in a draughty old shed with a leaking roof, freezing in winter and stifling in summer. For years Marie stirred huge pots of boiling material with an iron rod almost as tall as herself, then purified the results again and again.

After years of exhausting work, they finally isolated a small amount of radium. Marie went on to become the first person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.

Her success came not from perfect conditions but from extraordinary persistence. Waiting for ideal circumstances can be an excuse; great work is often done in imperfect places by people who simply refuse to stop.
source: Kể lại từ giai thoại lịch sử về Marie Curie

title: Edison's Thousand Experiments
text:
In the late 1870s, Thomas Edison and his team set out to build a practical electric light bulb. The main challenge was the filament, the thin thread inside the bulb that glows when electricity passes through it. Most materials either burnt out within seconds or melted.

The team tested an enormous range of materials, including platinum, cotton thread, paper and even hair. Thousands of experiments ended in failure. Many people would have lost heart, but Edison treated each failed test as useful information. Every material that did not work narrowed down the search.

Eventually they found that carbonised bamboo could glow for over a thousand hours. Electric lighting soon spread into homes and streets across the world.

Edison's real strength was not a single brilliant idea but a systematic, patient process of trial and error. Failure, approached in the right way, is simply part of the path to success.

title: Newton's Year at Home
text:
In 1665, a deadly plague swept through England, and Cambridge University closed its doors. A young student named Isaac Newton had to leave the city and return to his family's farm in the countryside.

Cut off from his teachers and lectures, he could easily have wasted the time. Instead, he used the quiet months to think deeply and work on his own. During this period he developed early ideas about calculus, carried out experiments with light and prisms, and began to think about why objects fall to the ground. The famous story of the falling apple, which he told in old age, is said to come from this time.

This period is now often called his "year of wonders".

A disruption to our normal routine can feel like a disaster. Yet with self-discipline and curiosity, it can become an opportunity to grow in ways we never expected.

title: Borrowing Light Through the Wall
text:
Kuang Heng grew up in a very poor family during the Han dynasty. He loved books, but his family could not afford candles, so once the sun went down, he had no way to read.

His neighbour, a wealthy man, kept lamps burning late into the night. One evening Kuang Heng noticed a thin line of light shining through a crack in the wall between their houses. Carefully, he chipped away at the crack until he had made a small hole. Then he held his book up to it and read by the faint light that came through.

Night after night he studied this way. He also worked for free for a rich family who owned many books, asking only to be allowed to read them in return. Eventually he became a respected scholar and a senior official.

Poverty can make learning harder, but a strong desire to learn will always find a way.
source: Kể lại từ giai thoại Trung Hoa về Khuông Hành

title: Demosthenes and the Pebbles
text:
Demosthenes, who lived in ancient Athens, dreamed of becoming a great public speaker. Unfortunately, he had a weak voice and a speech impediment, and his first speech in the assembly was greeted with laughter.

Rather than give up, he designed his own training programme. According to ancient writers, he practised speaking with pebbles in his mouth to force himself to pronounce words clearly. He recited speeches while running uphill to strengthen his breathing, and he spoke over the roar of the waves on the beach so that he could be heard above any noise. It is even said that he shaved half his head so that he would be too embarrassed to go out and would stay at home practising.

Years later, he became the most celebrated orator in Greece.

A weakness is not a final verdict. With deliberate practice, the very skill we are worst at can become our greatest strength.

title: Belling the Cat
text:
The mice in a large old house lived in constant fear of the cat. One night they held a meeting to discuss what could be done.

Many ideas were suggested and rejected. Finally a young mouse stood up with great confidence. "I have the perfect solution," he announced. "We will tie a bell round the cat's neck. Then, whenever she comes near, we will hear her and have time to escape."

The mice cheered loudly. It seemed like a brilliant plan. But when the noise died down, an old mouse who had been sitting quietly in the corner spoke up. "It is an excellent idea," he said. "Now tell me, which of you is going to put the bell on the cat?"

Nobody answered. The mice looked at each other in silence.

It is easy to propose solutions; it is much harder to carry them out. A plan is only as good as our ability to put it into practice.
source: Kể lại từ ngụ ngôn Aesop

title: The Ten-Minute Walk
text:
After years of long hours at his desk, Mr Hoang was told by his doctor that his blood pressure was too high. "You need to exercise," she said. He nodded, went home, and did nothing. Joining a gym felt like too big a commitment for someone so busy.

A month later, his daughter made a suggestion. "Don't try to change everything, Dad. Just walk around the lake for ten minutes after dinner. That's all."

Ten minutes seemed almost too easy, so he agreed. Some evenings it rained and he walked anyway. Soon ten minutes became twenty, because he was enjoying the fresh air and the chance to chat with neighbours. He began sleeping better and eating less late at night.

Six months later, his doctor was delighted with his results.

The secret was not willpower. It was starting with a habit so small that it was easier to do it than to make an excuse.
source: Truyện tự viết

title: The Oak and the Reeds
text:
A mighty oak stood beside a river, and next to it grew a cluster of thin reeds. The oak often looked down on them. "You poor things," it said. "The slightest breeze makes you bow. I, on the other hand, stand firm against any wind."

The reeds made no reply.

One night a violent storm swept down the valley. The oak refused to bend an inch. It held its branches stiffly against the gale, until at last, with a terrible crack, it was torn out by its roots and thrown into the river.

The reeds, meanwhile, bent low with every gust. When the storm passed, they simply stood up again, undamaged.

Strength is not always about resisting. Sometimes the wiser choice is to be flexible, adapt to the situation and wait for difficult times to pass.
source: Kể lại từ ngụ ngôn Aesop

title: The Voice Diary
text:
Lan worked in an office in Hanoi and wanted a higher IELTS score for a scholarship. Her reading was good, but whenever she had to speak English, her mind went blank.

One evening she decided to try something simple. Before bed, she recorded herself talking for two minutes about her day, in English, on her phone. The first recording was painful to listen to: long pauses, the same few words, and a lot of "um". She almost deleted it.

Instead, she kept going. Every night, another two minutes. Every Sunday she listened to the week's recordings, wrote down three mistakes she kept making, and tried to fix them the following week.

After two months, she played her first recording and her latest one side by side. She could hardly believe the difference. Her sentences were longer, her pauses shorter, and she sounded like herself.

Small, regular practice, reviewed honestly, beats occasional bursts of hard work.
source: Truyện tự viết

title: The Boy Who Cried Wolf
text:
A young shepherd boy was bored of watching sheep on the hillside all day. One afternoon, just for fun, he shouted, "Wolf! Wolf!" The villagers dropped their tools and ran up the hill to help, only to find the boy laughing at them.

A week later, he played the same trick. Again the villagers rushed up, and again there was no wolf. They walked home angry, warning him not to do it again.

Then one evening a real wolf crept out of the forest and began attacking the flock. The boy screamed for help at the top of his voice, but nobody came. Everyone assumed he was lying once more. By the time he got back to the village, many of the sheep were lost.

Trust takes a long time to build and only a moment to destroy. Once people stop believing you, even the truth sounds like a lie.
source: Kể lại từ ngụ ngôn Aesop

title: The North Wind and the Sun
text:
The North Wind and the Sun were arguing about which of them was stronger. Just then, they noticed a traveller walking along the road, wrapped in a warm cloak. They agreed that whoever could make him take off his cloak would be the winner.

The North Wind went first. He blew as hard as he could, sending icy blasts across the countryside. But the harder he blew, the more tightly the traveller held his cloak around him. Eventually the Wind gave up, exhausted.

Then it was the Sun's turn. He simply came out from behind the clouds and shone gently. The traveller began to feel warm. Before long, he loosened his cloak, and a little later he took it off altogether and sat down in the shade.

Persuasion often succeeds where force fails. People respond better to warmth and patience than to pressure.
source: Kể lại từ ngụ ngôn Aesop

title: The Notebook of Mistakes
text:
Minh hated getting his essays back. Each one came covered in red ink, and he usually glanced at the score, felt annoyed, and pushed the paper into a drawer.

One day his teacher noticed the pile of uncorrected work. "You are paying me to find your mistakes," she said, "and then you throw them away. That is like buying medicine and never taking it."

The comment stung, but it stayed with him. He bought a cheap notebook and started copying every mistake into it, with the correct version beside it. Before writing a new essay, he spent five minutes reading through the notebook.

At first the list grew quickly. Then something interesting happened: the same errors stopped appearing. Articles, verb tenses and missing plurals gradually disappeared from his work, and his scores began to rise.

Mistakes are not a sign of failure. They are free, personal lessons, but only if we take the time to study them.
source: Truyện tự viết
vi: Lỗi sai là bài học riêng miễn phí, nhưng chỉ có ích khi ta chịu dành thời gian xem lại.

title: The Fox and the Crow
text:
A crow had found a piece of cheese and flew up to a branch to enjoy it. A fox, passing below, saw the cheese and immediately wanted it for himself.

"Good morning, beautiful bird," he called. "What glossy feathers you have, and what bright eyes! Surely a creature so lovely must also have a wonderful voice. If only I could hear you sing just once, I would know you were the queen of all birds."

The crow was flattered. Eager to prove the fox right, she opened her beak and let out a loud caw. The cheese dropped straight to the ground, where the fox snapped it up.

"Thank you," said the fox as he trotted away. "In exchange for your cheese, here is some free advice: never trust a flatterer."

People who praise us too much often want something from us. Thinking critically, even about compliments, protects us from being manipulated.
source: Kể lại từ ngụ ngôn Aesop
vi: Kẻ nịnh hót thường muốn lợi dụng ta; hãy tỉnh táo, kể cả với lời khen.

title: The Lion and the Mouse
text:
A lion was sleeping in the forest when a little mouse accidentally ran across his face. The lion woke with a roar and trapped the mouse under his huge paw.

"Please let me go," begged the mouse. "One day I may be able to repay your kindness." The idea that such a tiny creature could ever help him amused the lion so much that he laughed and released her.

Some time later, the lion was caught in a hunter's net. The more he struggled, the tighter the ropes became, and his roars echoed through the trees. The mouse heard him and came running. Without wasting a second, she began gnawing through the ropes with her sharp teeth until the lion was free.

"You laughed at me," said the mouse, "but now you know that even a mouse can help a lion."

No act of kindness is ever wasted, and no one is too small to make a difference.
source: Kể lại từ ngụ ngôn Aesop
vi: Không lòng tốt nào là phí; ai cũng có thể tạo nên khác biệt, dù nhỏ bé đến đâu.

title: The Ant and the Grasshopper
text:
All summer long, a grasshopper sang and danced in the sunny fields. Nearby, an ant worked from dawn to dusk, carrying grains of wheat back to her nest one at a time.

"Why work so hard?" the grasshopper asked. "There is food everywhere. Come and enjoy yourself."

"I am storing food for the winter," the ant replied, "and I suggest you do the same." The grasshopper simply laughed and went back to his music.

Then winter arrived. Snow covered the ground, and the grasshopper, weak with hunger, knocked on the ant's door to beg for something to eat. The ant looked at him and asked what he had been doing all summer.

"I was singing," he admitted.

The story is not really about refusing to have fun. It is about planning ahead: the effort we make when life is easy is what protects us when times get hard.
source: Kể lại từ ngụ ngôn Aesop
vi: Hãy chuẩn bị khi mọi thứ còn thuận lợi; nỗ lực hôm nay là sự bảo vệ cho ngày khó khăn.

text: The important thing is not to stop questioning. Curiosity has its own reason for existing.

title: The Hare and the Tortoise
text:
A hare who was famous for his speed laughed at a tortoise for being so slow. Tired of the insults, the tortoise calmly challenged him to a race. The other animals gathered to watch, certain that the result was a foregone conclusion.

The hare shot ahead and was soon out of sight. Halfway along the course, he decided he had plenty of time to spare, so he lay down under a tree and fell fast asleep. Meanwhile, the tortoise kept going, one slow step after another, without ever stopping to rest.

When the hare finally woke up, the sun was setting. He sprinted towards the finish line as fast as his legs could carry him, but it was too late. The tortoise had already crossed it, and the crowd was cheering.

Talent can give you a head start, but it is steady effort that carries you to the end.
source: Kể lại từ ngụ ngôn Aesop
vi: Tài năng chỉ cho bạn lợi thế ban đầu; sự bền bỉ đều đặn mới đưa bạn tới đích.

title: The Goose That Laid the Golden Eggs
text:
A poor farmer and his wife owned a goose. One morning, to their amazement, they found that she had laid an egg made of solid gold. The next morning there was another, and the morning after that, another. Soon the couple were becoming rich.

But the richer they grew, the less patient they became. "One egg a day is far too slow," the farmer complained. "The goose must be full of gold inside. If we cut her open, we can take it all at once."

So they killed the goose. To their horror, she was just like any other goose inside. There was no gold at all, and now there would never be another golden egg.

Greed and impatience often destroy the very thing that gives us value. In study, health and business alike, the slow, steady source of benefit is usually worth more than a quick, one-off gain.
source: Kể lại từ ngụ ngôn Aesop
vi: Lòng tham và sự nóng vội có thể phá huỷ chính nguồn lợi lâu dài của mình.

title: The Farmer and His Sons
text:
An old farmer knew he did not have long to live. He called his sons, who were rather lazy, to his bedside. "My sons," he said, "there is a great treasure hidden in our vineyard. Dig, and you will find it."

After their father died, the sons took their spades and dug up every inch of the vineyard. They turned the soil over and over, searching for gold, but they found nothing at all. Disappointed, they decided the old man must have been confused.

However, because the soil had been so thoroughly dug and loosened, the vines grew stronger than ever that year. When autumn came, the harvest was the richest the family had ever seen. They sold the grapes and earned a small fortune.

Only then did the sons realise what their father had meant. The real treasure was not buried in the ground; it was the reward of hard work.
source: Kể lại từ ngụ ngôn Aesop
vi: Kho báu thật sự là thành quả của lao động chăm chỉ.

title: The Bundle of Sticks
text:
An old farmer had several sons who were always quarrelling. He had tried many times to persuade them to live in harmony, but his words had little effect.

One day he called them together and handed them a bundle of sticks tied tightly with string. "Break this," he said. Each son tried in turn, pushing with all his strength, but none of them could snap the bundle.

Then the father untied the string and gave each son a single stick. They broke them easily, one after another.

"You see," said the old man, "if you stand together and support one another, no enemy can defeat you. But if you are divided, you will be broken as easily as these sticks."

The sons looked at the pieces in their hands and understood. A team, a family or a community is strongest when its members work together instead of against each other.
source: Kể lại từ ngụ ngôn Aesop
vi: Đoàn kết thì mạnh, chia rẽ thì dễ bị đánh gục.

title: Pulling Up the Seedlings
text:
In ancient China there lived a farmer who was terribly impatient. Every morning he walked to his field to look at his young rice plants, and every morning he felt they had hardly grown at all.

One day he had an idea. He went along the rows and gently pulled each seedling up a little, so that it stood taller than before. It took him the whole day. That evening he came home exhausted but proud. "I have helped the rice to grow," he told his family.

His son ran out to the field to see. To his dismay, every single plant had wilted, because their roots no longer reached the soil properly.

Some things simply cannot be rushed. A language, a skill or a healthy body grows at its own pace, and trying to force quick results can undo all the progress we have made.
source: Kể lại từ truyện dân gian Trung Hoa (sách Mạnh Tử)
vi: Nóng vội đốt cháy giai đoạn sẽ làm hỏng việc; mọi thứ cần thời gian để lớn lên.

title: The Old Man Who Lost His Horse
text:
An old man lived near the northern border of China. One day his only horse ran away across the frontier. His neighbours came to comfort him, but he simply said, "Who knows whether this is bad luck?"

A few months later, the horse returned, bringing with it a magnificent wild stallion. The neighbours congratulated him. "Who knows whether this is good luck?" he replied.

His son loved riding the new stallion, but one day he fell off and broke his leg badly. Once again the neighbours expressed their sympathy, and once again the old man said, "Who knows whether this is bad luck?"

The following year, war broke out. Officers came to the village and took every healthy young man to fight. Most of them never returned. The old man's son, still limping, was left at home.

It is often impossible to judge an event while it is happening. Misfortune and fortune are closely connected.
source: Kể lại từ truyện dân gian Trung Hoa (Tái Ông thất mã)
vi: Tái ông mất ngựa, chưa biết là hoạ hay phúc; đừng vội phán xét một sự việc khi nó còn đang diễn ra.

title: The Frog in the Well
text:
A frog lived at the bottom of an old well. Every day he splashed in the shallow water and gazed up at the small circle of sky above him. He was perfectly content and believed he lived in the finest place in the world.

One day a sea turtle came to rest at the edge of the well. "Come down and join me," the frog called proudly. "My kingdom is wonderful. I am the master of all this water."

The turtle tried to climb in, but the well was far too narrow. So instead, he described the sea: water stretching further than the eye can see, so deep that no flood could raise it and no drought could lower it.

The frog was stunned. For the first time, he realised how small his world had been.

When we stay in one place and never seek new knowledge, we may mistake our narrow view for the whole truth.
source: Kể lại từ truyện ngụ ngôn Trung Hoa (sách Trang Tử)
vi: Ếch ngồi đáy giếng coi trời bằng vung; đừng nhầm tầm nhìn hạn hẹp của mình là toàn bộ sự thật.

title: Studying by Firefly Light
text:
Mac Dinh Chi, who lived in Vietnam in the thirteenth century, came from such a humble background that his family could not afford oil for a lamp. Yet he was determined to study.

According to popular tradition, he caught fireflies in the evenings and put them inside an eggshell with small holes in it. The tiny insects gave off just enough light for him to read a few lines at a time. When the fireflies grew dim, he would go out and catch more.

People in his village sometimes laughed at the small boy squinting at his books in the dark. He ignored them and kept going. Years later, he came first in the royal examination and became a famous scholar and diplomat, admired even by the Chinese court for his intelligence and wit.

The story reminds us that excuses are always available, but so is a way forward if we look for it hard enough.
source: Kể lại từ giai thoại Việt Nam về Mạc Đĩnh Chi

title: Franklin's Little Book of Virtues
text:
As a young man, Benjamin Franklin decided he wanted to improve his character. He wrote down thirteen virtues he hoped to develop, including order, frugality, sincerity and silence, which for him meant avoiding pointless talk.

He soon realised that trying to master all thirteen at once was overwhelming. So he made a small book with a chart for each week. He would concentrate on just one virtue a week, while keeping an eye on the others. Every evening he marked a small black spot next to any virtue he had failed at that day. After thirteen weeks, he would start the cycle again.

Franklin admitted that he never achieved perfection. The book was always full of spots. But he believed the effort made him a better and happier man than he would otherwise have been.

Tracking a habit daily makes progress visible, and focusing on one change at a time makes it manageable.
source: Kể lại từ giai thoại lịch sử về Benjamin Franklin
vi: Theo dõi thói quen hằng ngày giúp thấy tiến bộ; tập trung từng thay đổi một giúp dễ kiểm soát.

title: The Blind Men and the Elephant
text:
Six blind men had heard about a creature called an elephant, but none of them knew what it was like. One day an elephant was brought to their village, and they went to examine it.

The first man touched its side and declared, "An elephant is like a wall." The second felt its tusk. "No, it is like a spear." The third held the trunk and insisted it was like a snake. The fourth hugged a leg and said it was clearly a tree. The fifth touched an ear and was sure it was a fan, while the sixth grabbed the tail and laughed. "You are all wrong. It is a rope."

They argued for hours, each convinced he was right. In a sense, every one of them was partly right, and all of them were wrong.

We often mistake our own limited experience for the complete picture. Listening to other perspectives helps us see more of the truth.
source: Kể lại từ truyện dân gian Ấn Độ
vi: Thầy bói xem voi: mỗi người chỉ thấy một phần; lắng nghe góc nhìn khác giúp thấy sự thật đầy đủ hơn.

title: The Brothers Who Learnt to Fly
text:
Wilbur and Orville Wright were not university scientists. They ran a small bicycle shop in Ohio and had little formal training in engineering. Yet they became fascinated by the idea of human flight.

Instead of trying to build a powerful flying machine straight away, they focused on one problem at a time. They studied how birds balanced in the air, built their own wind tunnel to test wing shapes, and made hundreds of glider flights on the windy sand dunes of North Carolina. Each crash taught them something new, and they kept careful records of every result.

On 17 December 1903, Orville made the first powered, controlled flight. It lasted just twelve seconds and covered about 37 metres, but it changed the world.

The brothers succeeded by breaking a huge challenge into small, testable steps and learning patiently from every mistake.
source: Kể lại từ giai thoại lịch sử về anh em nhà Wright
vi: Chia thử thách lớn thành từng bước nhỏ có thể kiểm chứng, và kiên nhẫn học từ mọi sai lầm.

title: Waiting by the Tree Stump
text:
A farmer in the state of Song was working in his field when a rabbit came racing past, crashed straight into a tree stump and died on the spot. The farmer could hardly believe his good fortune. He picked up the rabbit, took it home, and enjoyed a delicious dinner.

The next morning, instead of picking up his hoe, he went and sat beside the stump. "If one rabbit ran into it," he reasoned, "another will surely come."

He waited all day. No rabbit came. He waited the next day, and the next. Weeks passed, and he sat there patiently while weeds took over his field. No more rabbits ever appeared, and the whole kingdom laughed at him.

A lucky break may happen once, but it is not a strategy. Relying on chance instead of effort is a sure way to lose what we already have.
source: Kể lại từ ngụ ngôn Trung Hoa (sách Hàn Phi Tử)

title: Empty Your Cup
text:
A university professor once visited a famous Zen master to learn about Zen. As soon as he sat down, the professor began talking about everything he already knew: the books he had read, the theories he had studied, the opinions he held.

The master listened quietly and began to pour tea. He filled the professor's cup to the brim, and then kept pouring. Tea spilled over the edge, across the table and onto the floor.

"Stop!" cried the professor. "It is overflowing. No more will go in!"

"Like this cup," the master said gently, "you are full of your own ideas. How can I show you anything new unless you first empty your cup?"

This is a valuable lesson for any learner. If we arrive convinced that we already understand, we leave no room for new knowledge. An open mind is the first requirement for real learning.
source: Kể lại từ giai thoại Thiền Nhật Bản

title: Archimedes and the King's Crown
text:
King Hiero of Syracuse once ordered a crown of pure gold. When it arrived, he suspected that the goldsmith had secretly mixed in cheaper silver. He asked the mathematician Archimedes to find out the truth without damaging the crown.

Archimedes thought about the problem for days without success. Then one day, as he stepped into a full bath, he noticed the water rising and spilling over the side. Suddenly he realised that an object pushes aside an amount of water equal to its own volume. Silver is lighter than gold, so a crown mixed with silver would take up more space than pure gold of the same weight.

According to the legend, he was so excited that he leapt out of the bath and ran through the streets shouting, "Eureka!" which means "I have found it!"

Great ideas often arrive when we relax, but only after we have thought hard about a problem.
source: Kể lại từ giai thoại lịch sử về Archimedes

title: The Foolish Old Man Who Moved the Mountains
text:
Long ago, an old man of ninety lived with his family behind two enormous mountains. Every time they went to town, they had to make a long journey around them. Finally he gathered his sons and grandsons and announced, "We will dig the mountains away."

They began carrying rocks and earth, basket by basket, to the distant sea. A round trip took them a whole season.

A neighbour, known for his cleverness, mocked him. "You are so old you can hardly lift a stone. How can you possibly move two mountains?"

The old man replied calmly, "When I die, my sons will carry on. Their sons will continue, and so will their grandsons. Our family will go on for ever, but the mountains will not grow any higher. Why should we fail?"

The clever neighbour had nothing to say. In the legend, the gods were so moved by this determination that they lifted the mountains away.
source: Kể lại từ truyện dân gian Trung Hoa (sách Liệt Tử)

title: The Merchant Who Read Aloud
text:
Heinrich Schliemann, the nineteenth-century businessman who later searched for the ancient city of Troy, was famous for his talent with languages. In his autobiography, he described his method.

Working as a poor office clerk in Amsterdam, he had little money for lessons. So he read aloud a great deal, never translated, wrote short essays on topics that interested him, and had them corrected by a teacher. The next day he learnt the corrected versions by heart and recited them. He even stood in queues at the post office mouthing passages, so that no minute was wasted.

He claimed that, using this method, he could reach a good level in a new language within months. Whether or not he exaggerated, the core of his approach still makes sense today.

Regular reading aloud, writing and getting feedback on our mistakes is a reliable route to fluency.
source: Kể lại từ giai thoại lịch sử về Heinrich Schliemann

title: The Dog and Its Reflection
text:
A dog had stolen a juicy piece of meat from a butcher's shop and was hurrying home to eat it in peace. On the way, he had to cross a narrow bridge over a calm stream.

As he looked down, he saw his own reflection in the water. He did not realise it was himself. Instead, he thought he was looking at another dog carrying an even bigger piece of meat.

Determined to have both, he growled and snapped at the other dog, opening his mouth wide to grab the second piece. Immediately, his own meat fell into the stream with a splash and sank out of sight. The reflection vanished, and the dog was left with nothing at all.

When we are never satisfied with what we have, we risk losing it. Comparing ourselves endlessly with others, especially online, can make us forget the value of what is already ours.
source: Kể lại từ ngụ ngôn Aesop

title: Robert the Bruce and the Spider
text:
In the early fourteenth century, Robert the Bruce, King of Scots, had been defeated in battle several times and was forced into hiding. According to a well-known legend, he lay in a cold, damp cave, wondering whether he should abandon his fight altogether.

As he sat there, he noticed a spider trying to spin a web across the entrance. It swung on its thread towards the wall but missed. It tried again, and failed again. Six times the spider failed. Robert watched, thinking of his own six defeats.

On the seventh attempt, the spider reached the wall and fixed its thread. Its web was complete.

The king took this as a sign. He left the cave, gathered his followers, and in the end won a famous victory that secured Scotland's independence.

Whether or not the story is true, its message is clear: one more attempt can be the one that succeeds.
source: Kể lại từ truyền thuyết Scotland

title: The Milkmaid and Her Pail
text:
A young milkmaid was walking to market with a pail of fresh milk balanced on her head. As she walked, she began to daydream.

"With the money from this milk, I will buy some eggs," she thought. "The eggs will hatch into chickens, and I will sell the chickens to buy a beautiful new dress. When I wear it to the fair, all the young men will want to dance with me. But I shall simply toss my head and walk away."

At that moment, carried away by her daydream, she tossed her head proudly. The pail fell to the ground, and all the milk spilled into the dust. Her eggs, her chickens and her new dress vanished in an instant.

There is nothing wrong with dreaming about the future, but we should not count our chickens before they hatch. Plans only become real when we pay attention to the step in front of us.
source: Kể lại từ ngụ ngôn Aesop

title: Grinding an Iron Rod into a Needle
text:
When the poet Li Bai was a boy, he found his studies dull and often sneaked out of class. One afternoon, wandering by a stream, he came across an old woman rubbing a thick iron rod against a large stone.

"Grandmother, what are you doing?" he asked.

"I am making a needle," she replied, without looking up.

Li Bai burst out laughing. "A needle? From that great piece of iron? It will take you forever!"

The old woman smiled. "If I grind a little every day, and never stop, one day it will be thin enough. The only thing that could stop me is giving up."

The boy fell silent. He walked back to school and, according to the legend, studied with new determination from that day on, eventually becoming one of the greatest poets in Chinese history.

With enough persistence, even an impossible task can be broken down and completed.
source: Kể lại từ giai thoại dân gian Trung Hoa về Lý Bạch

title: Fleming's Untidy Laboratory
text:
In September 1928, the Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming returned to his London laboratory after a summer holiday. He had left several dishes of bacteria on his bench, and when he looked at them, he noticed something odd.

A blue-green mould had started growing on one dish, and around it, the bacteria had died. Many scientists would have thrown the spoilt dish away without a second thought. Fleming, however, was curious. He grew the mould, studied it carefully and discovered that it produced a substance that killed many harmful bacteria. He called it penicillin.

It took more than a decade, and the work of other scientists, to turn penicillin into a medicine that could be mass-produced. Since then, antibiotics have saved countless lives.

Discoveries often begin with an accident, but they only happen when someone pays close attention and asks, "Why?"
source: Kể lại từ giai thoại lịch sử về Alexander Fleming
